<bot> even with a fast processor?<endOfText>
<human> yes, the disks are the limiting factor<endOfText>
<bot> how so, is it their seek time?<endOfText>
<human> with raid5 over 3 disks, the read actions are nicely spread over all 3 disks, the writes however results writes on 2 or even 3 disks simultaneously: not much performance gain over a single disk<endOfText>
<bot> what can i do increase the speed?<endOfText>
<human> more disks ;)<endOfText>
<bot> so if i add another disk to the raid 5 array it will be faster on the writes?<endOfText>
<human> though write performance will never be really great with raid5, if you want both read and write performance, go for raid10<endOfText>
<bot> it also highly depends on your io patterns<endOfText>
<human> the real performance gains with raid5 are when using a hardware raid controller with a battery backed write chache<endOfText>
<bot> or use SSDs ;)<endOfText>
<human> i have a ssd can i use that as  a cache,  how do i use a cache?<endOfText>
<bot> only highend hardware raid controllers can use ssds as cache (and you'd need an enterprise class ssd for that as well), zfs can use ssds as cache as well though<endOfText>
<human> what about lvm<endOfText>
<bot> wont make a difference afaik<endOfText>
<human> when write performance is needed, one usually just doesnt use raid5 :)<endOfText>
<bot> do you think i should buy an other disk and switch to raid10?<endOfText>
<human> it all comes down to your needs/wishes/wallet basically, but raid10 is quite likely to give you much better write performance than raid5<endOfText>

<human> g++ -l/usr/include/ -Wall -c hello-world.c<endOfText>
<bot> Yeah, an object file isn't executable.<endOfText>
<human> The '-c' option to g++ explicitely tells it to compile only and not link.  If you either omit it (and use a.out) or you specify an output with -o, you'll get a linked executable.<endOfText>
<bot> In fact, if you either omit -c or use -o, you'll note that g++ will have automatically marked the file with the +x flag.<endOfText>
<human> ok, so using -o will fix it?<endOfText>
<bot> The main thing is to leave off the -c.  Or if you want, you can do:  'g++ -c hello-world.c; g++ -o hello hello-world.o'  The second command takes your object file and links it into an executable.<endOfText>
<human> For such a simple project (single file), there isn't much point to doing it in two steps though.<endOfText>

<bot> Ok, on Gparted, how will i be able to tell which partition is ubuntu and which is windows 7<endOfText>

<bot> the recovery will likely be smaller<endOfText>
<human> ther eis also traditionally a label<endOfText>
<bot> its not a bad idea to backup before resizing, but otherwise it should be safe. it will take a long time to shrink the partition because the data has to be moved<endOfText>
<human> one headache you will have is that extended partition. you can shrink the ext4 and then move it back so that there is blank space between the end of sda2 and the start of sda5, but you cannot expand the sda2 without shrinking the extended<endOfText>
<bot> a couple of approaches at that point would be to (a) take a backup of your partition table and then delete it, and recreate a new one that matches the current partition table exactly, but has the extended partition starting later<endOfText>
<human> alternately you could use a tool like gdisk to convert the mbr table to a gpt table and then convert from gpt back to mbr setting the extended partition as desired<endOfText>
<bot> start by shrinking sda5. the shrink will happen at the end of sda5 leaving blank space between sda5 and sda6. then move sda5 so that it lines up with sda6. now you have blank space inside sda4 (its that extended container)<endOfText>
<human> then you would want to resize the extended partition (you shrunk the boxes inside the extended partition box so now you can shrink the extended partition box itself) but the tools might not let you do that<endOfText>
<bot> and so you might have to work around that, and the two ways are to backup the table and create a new one, or to convert from mbr->gpt->mbr<endOfText>

Linux might see hard drives as scsi or 'hard drive' devices,  More modern ones will see everything as scsi devices.  The first hard disk is given the letter a, the next b, and so on, but for 'ide' hard drives Primary Master == a, Secondary Master == C, and the slaves for each are B and D respectively...<endOfText>

<bot> why does old software releases like firefox or Java Webstart are shown by the package manager as updated but aren't in their latest version?<endOfText>
<human> the versions of the programs in the repositories lag behind the actual version of the program made by the developer<endOfText>
<bot> the repositories are maintained by others<endOfText>
<human> older versions are left in the repositories due to stability concerns.  security updates are then backported so that those older versions are just as stable but have security fixes.  then after a while they will just use the newer version once it has been proven stable<endOfText>
<bot> so if I want to update those programs, how can i make ir w/o interfiering with the package manager?<endOfText>
<human> it's a little messy<endOfText>
<bot> i usually just uninstall the repository version first<endOfText>
<human> :O very interesting<endOfText>
<bot> then install the latest version manually.  the package manager won't know it's there<endOfText>
<human> in wich directory should I install the new applications?<endOfText>
<bot> /usr/local generally<endOfText>
<human> I see, it's better to install the updated apps manually or it's better to just stick with the package manager?<endOfText>
<bot> better to stick with the package manager unless you absolutely need the latest version of the app<endOfText>
